name: Anne Frank House and the Prinsengracht
label: Anne Frank House
camera_source: Commons cluster (7 photos), weak. Moved 20 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 25 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/601081859: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Anne Frank House' (57 m across).
notes: Photography inside is not allowed (to be checked); the spot is the canal-side front.

text.description:
The Anne Frank House is the canal house on the Prinsengracht where Anne Frank and seven others hid from Nazi persecution during the Second World War. Today it is a museum. From the street it looks like a tall, narrow canal house with a plain front, which is part of why it photographs so well. It fits the row of neighbouring houses, the water and the bridges along the canal, so a single frame can show both the building and the street it belongs to.

The house was built in 1635 by Dirk van Delft, and the canal-side front dates from a renovation in 1740. The hiding place, the Secret Annex, is in the rear building and cannot be seen from the street. The museum opened on 3 May 1960 and now takes in the neighbouring houses at numbers 263 to 267. In 2017 it had about 1.27 million visitors, so the street outside may be busy at times.

The phone icon on the map is about 25 m south-west of the subject. From there you can include the canal edge, the neighbouring gables and some sky without pointing the phone steeply upwards. Keep the phone level and use the gridlines so the vertical lines of the building stay straight. If people are in the foreground, wait a moment for a gap, or include them on purpose to show the scale of the place. The Westerkerk is close by if you want a second frame. Please be quiet and respectful around the entrance, and check the official site before you go for entry rules and any photography rules inside.
text.geographic_location: On the Prinsengracht at number 263 to 267, close to the Westerkerk, in central Amsterdam (about 52.37515 N, 4.88409 E).
text.directions_text: Trams are usually the easiest way to get here (GVB runs both trams and metro). The nearest stop is Marnixplein (tram 13, tram 5), about 8 minutes on foot, with the house to the south-east. Bloemgracht (tram 13, tram 5) is about 9 minutes on foot, with the house to the east. From Rokin (metro 52, tram 14, tram 4) it is about 13 minutes on foot, heading north-west. From Centraal Station (metro 51, metro 52, metro 53, metro 54, tram 14, tram 17, tram 2, tram 24, tram 26, tram 4) it is about 19 minutes on foot, heading west. Once you reach the Prinsengracht, the phone icon on the map is the place to stop for your photo. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

If the pavement is narrow and you cannot step back, try the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level so the house does not lean. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the windows, shutters and the doorway area.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the front of the house to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the brickwork stays rich and the sky is not washed out. Live Photos can help you pick a frame with fewer passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day usually means fewer people on the pavement. Soft, even light on an overcast day suits the dark front of the house, and evening gives a quieter mood by the water, where night mode can help.

label: Rijksmuseum

text.description:
The Rijksmuseum is the national museum of the Netherlands, and its main building was designed by Pierre Cuypers. The architect mixed gothic and renaissance ideas, so the red-brick front has pointed roofs, towers, decorative bands and lots of detail. It opened in 1885. After a ten-year renovation, it reopened in April 2013. The museum shows around 8,000 objects, including works by Rembrandt, Frans Hals and Vermeer. It sits on Museumplein, beside the Van Gogh Museum, the Stedelijk Museum and the Concertgebouw, so the open square gives you room to step back and fit the whole building in.

The phone icon on the map is about 140 m west of the subject. From there you can take in the full width of the façade and its towers, with the surrounding space in the frame. The building is big, so a wide shot works best, then move closer and pick out details such as the roofline, the windows and the brickwork. Walking around the square also gives you different foregrounds, such as people, trees and the open paving. Keep your phone level so the tall vertical lines don't lean inwards.
text.geographic_location: The Rijksmuseum stands on Museumplein in the Amsterdam South borough. It is close to the Van Gogh Museum, the Stedelijk Museum and the Royal Concertgebouw.
text.directions_text: Trams are usually the easiest way to get here. The nearest stop is Rijksmuseum (tram 1, tram 7 and tram 19), and the museum is to the south-west, about 3 minutes on foot. Museumplein stop (tram 2, tram 5 and tram 24) is about 5 minutes on foot, with the museum to the north-east. Vijzelgracht metro station (metro 52, also tram 1, tram 7 and tram 19) is about 7 minutes on foot, with the museum to the west. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole façade and the open space around it. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for towers, rooflines and decorative details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From there you can see the full front of the museum without turning.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up so the verticals stay straight. Put the museum in the centre or slightly to one side, and leave some empty space in front of it so it doesn't feel crowded. For variety, try a closer shot with the 2x telephoto, focusing on the towers and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks too bright. If it is cloudy, keep the sky small in the frame so it doesn't look washed out. Use panorama only if you can keep your phone steady, as it can distort straight lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. At dusk, night mode can capture the building with its lights on, but hold the phone very still.

name: Vondelpark
label: Vondelpark
camera_source: Commons cluster (6 photos), weak.

text.description:
Vondelpark is a large public city park in Amsterdam, and an easy place to fill a phone gallery. It covers 47 hectares in the Amsterdam-Zuid district, just west of the Museumplein and Leidseplein. It opened in 1865 as 'the New Park' and was later named after the 17th-century poet Joost van den Vondel, whose statue of 1867 still stands there. The Zocher family designed it in the English landscape style, so the paths curve gently and the lawns, trees and water open out in soft layers, which is exactly what a phone likes. It became a state monument (rijksmonument) in 1996 and welcomes around 10 million visitors a year, so expect people in your frames.

There is plenty to point a camera at besides the greenery. The round, modernist Blauwe Theehuis (Blue Tearoom) dates from 1937. Picasso's sculpture 'The Fish' was placed here in 1965. The big pond and the Vondelpark Pavilion (built in 1878) make good backdrops. Walk the paths and pick scenes with a clear foreground, such as a curving path, a bench or a patch of water, and a line of trees behind it. Keep a little distance from strangers and picnics, and shoot people from behind or as small figures if you want a calm picture. The phone icon on the map gives you a good first view.
text.geographic_location: Vondelpark lies in the Amsterdam-Zuid district, west of the Leidseplein and the Museumplein.
text.directions_text: The nearest stops are tram stops, and trams (run by GVB) are usually the easiest way to get here. Take tram 2 to Cornelis Schuytstraat, with Vondelpark to the north-west, about 5 minutes on foot. Or take tram 1 to Jan Pieter Heijestraat, with Vondelpark to the south-east, about 5 minutes on foot. If you prefer the metro, metro 52 stops at De Pijp (also tram 12 and tram 25) and at Vijzelgracht (also tram 1, tram 19 and tram 7). Both are to the east of the park, with Vondelpark to the west, and about 26 minutes on foot, so the tram is much easier. The phone icon on the map is about 280 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for paths, benches and the tearoom as people see them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for open lawns or the pond when you want the whole scene. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for statues, ducks and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 280 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Stop where a path curves, or where water and trees line up, rather than shooting straight across an empty lawn.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the path or water edge on a lower third line. Use trees on one side as a natural frame. With ultra-wide, keep the horizon level and avoid putting people at the edges, where they stretch. Use portrait mode for a friend or a sculpture against soft greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Dappled shade can fool the camera, so check the result and retake if faces are too dark. Live Photos work well for moving water or cyclists passing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Weekday mornings are generally quieter than sunny weekend afternoons.

text.access_note: Vondelpark is a public park; check the official site before you go for events, the open-air theatre season (June to August) and any rules.

name: Dam Square and the Royal Palace
label: Dam Square

text.description: Dam Square is the open heart of old Amsterdam, and it is one of the easiest places in the city to photograph because so much is gathered around one wide space. The square began as a dam on the River Amstel built around 1270, which is where the city's name comes from. Today it is a big rectangle, roughly 200 metres from west to east, with several tram lines running through it. At the west end stands the neoclassical Royal Palace, which was the city hall from 1655 until it became a royal residence in 1808. The 15th-century Gothic Nieuwe Kerk sits beside it. Facing them on the other side of the square is the white stone National Monument, designed by J.J.P. Oud and put up in 1956 to remember the victims of the Second World War. The mix of grand stonework, old church architecture and city life gives you plenty of variety without moving far. Then look back towards the west end and try the palace façade as a separate shot. Wait a moment for people to move out of the way, and keep the horizon straight, because the big buildings look odd when they lean.
text.geographic_location: Dam Square is in Amsterdam's historic centre, between the streets Damrak and Rokin. The subject on the map is the National Monument, in the square itself.
text.directions_text: Amsterdam has metro lines and many trams, both run by GVB, and trams are usually the easiest. The nearest stop is Dam (tram 14, tram 17, tram 2, tram 24 and tram 4), about 3 minutes on foot, with the subject to the south. Paleisstraat (tram 17, tram 2 and tram 24) is about 4 minutes on foot, with the subject to the east. The nearest metro is Rokin (metro 52, plus tram 14 and tram 4), about 5 minutes on foot, with the subject to the north. From Nieuwmarkt (metro 51, metro 53 and metro 54) it is about 8 minutes on foot, heading west. Once you reach the square, walk to the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long square and the tall buildings into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the palace or the monument. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as the monument's pillar or the palace roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. For the Royal Palace, look towards the west end of the square and shoot from where you stand.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the lower line so the buildings and sky share the frame. Use a person or tram passing in the foreground to show scale. Keep your phone upright and level to stop the buildings leaning, and step back rather than tilting upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or stonework, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the light façades keep their detail. Try panorama mode for the full width of the square, moving slowly and steadily. Live Photos can catch passing trams and pigeons.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually the calmest time for clear wide shots. In the evening, switch on night mode, hold the phone steady against your body, and shoot the lit buildings after dusk.

text.access_note: The square itself is open public space; the Royal Palace and Nieuwe Kerk interiors may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: NEMO Science Museum is the big Renzo Piano building beside the water at the edge of Amsterdam's old centre. The museum began in 1923 and has been in this building since 1997. It has five floors of hands-on exhibits and is the largest science centre in the Netherlands. The subject is the building itself, and the spot is about two things: the building's bold shape, and the view from the upper deck on the fifth floor, which has a cafeteria, a children's play area and a view over the city. That makes it a good place for a wide city picture with a bit of the building in the foreground. Because the phone icon on the map is right at the building, you can walk around a little and try a few angles. Start with a wide frame to show the setting, then move closer for simple shots of lines and curves. Wipe your lens before you start, because fingerprints show up as haze when the sun is low. If you go up to the deck, avoid shooting through glass where you can. If you must, press the phone lens close to the pane to cut reflections. Access to the upper deck may depend on a ticket or opening times, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
A'DAM Lookout is a photo spot at the A'DAM Toren, the tall tower on Overhoeksplein in the Overhoeks area of Amsterdam Noord. It makes a good photo stop for two reasons. From the ground, the tower is a strong shape to point a phone at. If you go up, you may be able to look back towards the city and take a wide skyline picture that is hard to get from street level.

At the foot of the tower, the phone icon on the map puts you right beside the building. This is the place for a dramatic upward shot. Tilt the phone up and the tower's lines lead the eye towards the sky, which works especially well with clouds or colour behind it. If you go up to the lookout, take your pictures in layers: first a wide view of the whole skyline, then closer shots of single buildings, boats and rooftops.

Practical advice: wipe your phone lens before you start, as fingerprints cause hazy, smeared pictures. If you shoot through glass, press the lens close to it and shade the screen with your hand to cut reflections. Keep the phone level when you shoot the skyline, so the horizon stays straight. Take a few frames of each view, because people and boats keep moving through the scene. Whether you can go up, and when, may depend on tickets and opening times, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
The Jordaan is a neighbourhood of narrow streets, small canals and tall gabled houses, and it is one of the easiest parts of Amsterdam to enjoy with a phone in your hand. It was begun in 1612 under the name Het Nieuwe Werck (The New Work), and its streets follow older ditches and paths. That is why it sits at a different angle from the rest of the city, and why you keep finding unexpected corners and crooked views. Most of the streets and canals are named after trees and flowers, so look out for the names on the corner signs.

The photographs here come from the small details as much as the wide views. Many houses carry a carved stone tablet above the door showing a trade, such as a pig for a butcher or scissors for a tailor. The first of these were made in the 16th century. The area also has many hofjes, which are inner courtyards built as charity housing for elderly women. Many are now homes, so look from the entrance and keep your voice down. Some open on summer Sundays for free concerts.

Use the canal or street to lead the eye into the picture, and add a bicycle, a bridge or a doorway for scale. Then walk slowly and shoot the tablets, window boxes and house fronts up close. Markets are held at Noordermarkt, Westerstraat and Lindengracht, which can add colour if you are passing on a market day.
text.geographic_location: The Jordaan is a neighbourhood in the Amsterdam-Centrum borough, west of the Prinsengracht canal. It is bounded by the Brouwersgracht to the north, the Leidsegracht to the south and the Singelgracht to the west.

From Rokin station (metro 52, tram 14 and tram 4) it is about 17 minutes on foot to the north-west, and from Centraal Station (metro 51, metro 52, metro 53, metro 54, tram 14, tram 17, tram 2, tram 24, tram 26 and tram 4) it is about 21 minutes on foot to the west. shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bloemgracht (bridge at the Eerste Bloemdwarsstraat junction). A long view along the Bloemgracht's row of tall 17th-century merchant houses, with the water and bridge railings in the foreground. From there you can shoot along the street or canal towards it.

text.description: The Begijnhof is a quiet courtyard of tall, narrow Amsterdam houses around grassy areas, with a green on each side of the chapel, set just inside the Singel canal. It began as a béguinage, a community for religious women, and is one of the oldest courtyards of its kind in the city. It is also the only inner court in Amsterdam that dates from the Middle Ages. Today it is still mostly private homes, with two churches among them: the English Reformed Church and the Catholic Miracle Church. It photographs well because it feels so different from the busy streets outside. You get green space framed by 47 individual town houses, most with 17th- or 18th-century fronts, and many gable stones to look for. The house at number 34 is a restored wooden building dating from about 1420, said to be the oldest wooden house in Amsterdam. The ground here sits about a metre below the surrounding old centre, because it is still at medieval street level. For phone photos, keep the whole courtyard in one frame to show the setting, then move in for details such as gable stones, doorways and the wooden house. Remember that people live here, so keep your voice low and stay out of doorways and private entrances.
text.geographic_location: The Begijnhof is in Amsterdam's old centre, inside the Singel canal and close to the Rokin and Spui area. It is tucked behind the street frontage, so you reach it through a gateway.
text.directions_text: Amsterdam has metro lines and many trams, both run by GVB, and trams are usually the easiest. The nearest stop is Rokin (tram 14, tram 4 and metro 52): the Begijnhof is to the south-west, about 3 minutes on foot. From the Koningsplein tram stop (tram 17, tram 2 and tram 24) walk north for about 3 minutes on foot. From the Paleisstraat tram stop (tram 17, tram 2 and tram 24) walk south for about 5 minutes on foot. If you come from Nieuwmarkt (metro 51, metro 53 and metro 54), head west for about 13 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

The full courtyard with the gabled almshouse fronts and the chapel at the far end, with the garden beds in the foreground. Use it as your starting point, then head south-east into the courtyard. text.description:
Leidseplein is one of Amsterdam's best-known squares, and it is as much about atmosphere as architecture. It sits where the Weteringschans, Marnixstraat and Leidsestraat meet, just north-east of the Singelgracht. Long ago it was the end of the road from Leiden and served as a parking area for horse-drawn traffic. Today trams and other traffic cross it, and the side streets are lined with restaurants and clubs. It is counted among the busiest nightlife areas in the city.

The square photographs well because several things share one view: the Stadsschouwburg, the city's nationally renowned theatre and the most notable building here, the busy street life in front of it, and the American Hotel close by. A passing tram gives a good sense of movement and of the city, and the buildings give you strong lines to work with.

Try a wide view first to show the whole scene, then step in for a closer shot of the theatre facade or a tram crossing. text.description:
The Bloemenmarkt is a row of flower and souvenir stalls beside the Singel canal, and it is the world's only floating flower market. It was founded in 1862 and sits between Muntplein and Koningsplein in the southern canal belt. Today it has 15 souvenir and gift shops, and only a few still sell fresh flowers. Most of what you see is bulbs, tulip-themed gifts and trinkets.

For a good set of pictures, take one wide shot of the whole row, one mid-distance shot with the water in the foreground, and a few close-ups of the flowers and packets. Watch for other visitors passing in front of your phone, and wait a moment for a gap. If you plan to buy bulbs, bear in mind that a 2019 survey found bulbs bought here rarely to never flowered, so treat them as souvenirs. Shops and stalls may have their own rules about photographing the goods, so ask politely if you want to get very close.

text.description:
The Oude Kerk is Amsterdam's oldest parish church, and the oldest structure in the city. A wooden chapel stood here around 1213, and the stone church was consecrated in 1306. It became a Reformed church after the Reformation of 1578 and still is one today. It stands in De Wallen, on the Oudekerksplein.

The church is large, covering some 3,300 m2, so it is easier to capture in pieces than all at once. Take one wide shot to show the setting, then a few closer shots of the tower, the windows and the stonework.

Inside, the floor is made up of gravestones, and the ceiling is the largest medieval wooden vault in Europe. Each year on 9 March (8 March in leap years), at 8:39 am, early sun briefly lights the tomb of Rembrandt's wife Saskia. Whether you can photograph inside, and under what rules, is up to the church, so check the official site before you go. Outside, give yourself a few minutes: people pass through the square all the time, so wait for a gap and keep the church straight in the frame.

text.description:
Rembrandtplein is a broad, tree-edged square in central Amsterdam, and its centrepiece is the statue of Rembrandt standing on a grey granite base. The statue was made in 1852 by Louis Royer. It is cast iron, was cast in one piece, and is Amsterdam's oldest surviving statue in a public space. The square began as a medieval city gateway and later became a butter market. It was renamed in 1876, when the statue was moved to the centre.

It photographs well because the layout is simple. The statue sits in the middle of a paved plaza with planters, trees and a small fountain, and the surrounding buildings give you a lively backdrop. The large Bank building across Utrechtsestraat, designed in 1926, adds a solid, historic frame. The square has been a centre for nightlife since the early twentieth century, so the cafés and signs around it add colour after dark.

You may read about bronze Night Watch figures here. They were removed in February 2020, so don't plan a shot around them. Take the statue as your subject, keep the square's trees and buildings around it, and let people walking through add a sense of scale. Wipe your lens first, as phone lenses pick up smudges, and take a few frames with and without passers-by.

The extra draw is a replica of the Amsterdam, moored outside. The original was an 18th-century ship that sailed between the Netherlands and the East Indies, and the replica was built between 1985 and 1990. Its tall masts and rigging give the building a lively foreground, and they make a good contrast with the calm, square lines behind.

That is quite a distance, so think of this as a view of the whole scene rather than a close-up. Try to include some water or sky around the ship so it has room to breathe. name: Hortus Botanicus

camera_source: Commons cluster (81 photos).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/31527079: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hortus Botanicus' (235 m across).

text.description:
Hortus Botanicus is a botanical garden in the Plantage district, and one of the oldest in the world. Amsterdam City Council founded it in 1638 as a herb garden for doctors and apothecaries, who trained and sat exams there. The collection began with plants and seeds that Dutch East India Company traders brought home. A single coffee plant from the garden is said to have been the parent of coffee growing across Central and South America.

It photographs well because several periods sit close together. The hexagonal pavilion dates from the late 1600s and the entrance gate from the early 1700s. The Orangery was built in 1875, and the Palm House and the Hugo de Vries Laboratory (1912 and 1915) are in Amsterdam School style. Add the Snippendaal Garden of medicinal plants, a large hothouse with three tropical climates, and trees such as the Persian ironwood, and you have plenty to choose from, whether you want a wide scene or a close detail.

For a phone, think in layers: a leafy foreground, a path or building behind it, and sky above. Look for repeating shapes such as glass panes, palm fronds and brick lines. Inside the glasshouses, wipe your lens first, because humid air and fingerprints soften pictures. Take a few shots of each scene at different zoom settings, then pick the best one later. Check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.
text.geographic_location: In the Plantage district of Amsterdam. It lies to the east of Waterlooplein station and to the east of the Artis tram stop, and to the south-east of the Meester Visserplein tram stop.

Alternatively, take tram 14 to Artis, with the garden to the west of the stop, about 4 minutes on foot. Or go to Waterlooplein (metro 51, metro 53, metro 54 and tram 14), where the garden is to the east of the station, about 6 minutes on foot. shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits the plants and brickwork best. Overcast days also work well because colours stay even and glass reflects less glare.

text.description:
Damrak is the broad street that greets you as you leave Amsterdam Centraal, and the row of narrow, gabled houses along it is one of the easiest photos to get on arrival. The tall, slim fronts lean and step against each other, which gives the 'dancing' look the spot is named for. Behind them the street, a partly filled-in canal, runs straight towards the city centre, so you get plenty of depth in a single frame.

Damrak runs between the station and Dam Square. It follows a straight stretch (a 'rak') of the Amstel river near a dam, which is where the name comes from. Part of it was filled in during the 19th century. Today it is known for restaurants, bars and tourist shops, and canal boats still work its water, so a boat sliding through the foreground can add life to the picture. The former stock exchange, the Beurs van Berlage, stands along the street and is now a concert and exhibition hall.

For a phone shot, use the phone icon on the map. The houses are about 106 metres from it, to the east, so you will not need to walk far. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay upright, and wait a moment for pedestrians and trams to clear if you want a calmer frame. Pavements here are busy, so step out of the flow before you stop to shoot.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Amsterdam, on Damrak, the street that runs from Amsterdam Centraal towards Dam Square. The houses are around the middle of the street, about 290 metres south-west of Centraal Station.
text.directions_text: Start at Centraal Station (metro 51, metro 52, metro 53, metro 54, tram 2, tram 4, tram 14, tram 17, tram 24 or tram 26) and walk south-west for about 5 minutes on foot. By tram, you can instead get off at Nieuwezijds Kolk (tram 2, tram 17 or tram 24) and walk east for about 4 minutes on foot. Then follow the map to the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole row of houses and the street into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural, less stretched look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single gable or a canal boat.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line a house edge up with a vertical grid line so the buildings stand straight. Leave some street or water in the lower part of the frame to give a sense of depth. A passing boat or tram makes a good focal point.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest house front to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky and pale walls keep their detail. In the evening, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a post or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when there are fewer people on the pavements. Around dusk, shop and street lights add colour to the fronts.

text.access_note: This is an open public street, so you can photograph from the pavement at any time; if you want to go inside any building, check the official site before you go.

name: Magere Brug (Skinny Bridge)
label: Magere Brug
camera_source: Commons cluster (3 photos), weak. Moved 41 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 45 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.

text.description:
The Magere Brug, or Skinny Bridge, is a white wooden drawbridge across the River Amstel, at the point where Kerkstraat meets the river between the Keizersgracht and the Prinsengracht. It photographs well because the whole bridge fits neatly in one frame: pale timber, a lifting centre section and water on both sides. In the evening about 1,200 light bulbs come on and outline it against the dusk, which is when most visitors want a picture.

The first bridge here dates from 1691 and had 13 arches. Locals nicknamed it the skinny bridge because it was so narrow. The present bridge was built in 1934 to a design by Piet Kramer, and it has been limited to pedestrians and cyclists since 2003. The centre section lifts many times a day for river traffic, and it was operated by hand until 1994. Sightseeing boats are low enough to pass underneath when it is closed. Locals also think of it as Amsterdam's most romantic bridge.

From there you see it side-on with some of the river in front, so you get the whole structure without needing to be close. If the centre section lifts while you are there, keep shooting: a raised bridge with a boat passing makes a livelier picture. Expect cyclists and walkers crossing, so wait a moment for a gap, or let them add some life to the scene.
text.geographic_location: The Magere Brug crosses the River Amstel in central Amsterdam, linking the two banks at Kerkstraat between the Keizersgracht and the Prinsengracht. It lies about 364 m south of Waterlooplein, roughly 6 minutes on foot.
text.directions_text: Trams are usually the easiest way to get here, but the nearest stop of all is the Waterlooplein station (metro 51, metro 53, metro 54 and tram 14), about 6 minutes on foot, heading south. From Weesperplein (metro 51, metro 53, metro 54, tram 1, tram 19 and tram 7) it is about 8 minutes on foot, heading north-west. From the Rembrandtplein tram stop (tram 14 and tram 4) allow about 8 minutes on foot, heading south-east, and from the Frederiksplein tram stop (tram 1, tram 19, tram 4 and tram 7) about 8 minutes on foot, heading north-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand to get the whole bridge and some water in the frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the lifting section and the lights. Ultra-wide (0.5x) only works well if you walk closer, otherwise the bridge looks small and distant.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Amsteldijk (east bank of the Amstel, just south of the bridge). The full span of the white bridge centred in the frame, with its lit structure reflected in the river, especially after dark. Turn on the gridlines and line the bridge's deck up with a horizontal line.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place the bridge slightly off-centre and leave some water in the foreground. Keep the bridge's horizontal line level with the gridlines so it doesn't look tilted. If a boat approaches or the centre section lifts, take a few shots in a row. If you take Live Photos, you can pick the best moment later.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lit bulbs stay sharp and don't wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your phone on a wall or railing, if there is one, to stay steady. Moving boats and passers-by may blur in night mode, so take a few shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early evening, when the bulbs are on and the sky still has some colour, gives the most atmospheric result. Daytime also works if you want to show the white timber clearly.

text.access_note: The bridge is an open public crossing for pedestrians and cyclists, but check the official site before you go if you need details on any restrictions.

camera_source: Commons cluster (14 photos). Moved 4 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 45 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.

text.description: The Munttoren, or Mint Tower, is a slim tower with an eight-sided upper half and an open, lacy spire. It stands right where the Amstel river and the Singel canal meet, on the busy Muntplein square, so you get water, old brick and city bustle in one frame. It began as part of the Regulierspoort, a medieval city gate built around 1480. After a fire in 1618 only the guard house and part of the western tower remained standing. It was rebuilt in 1620 in Amsterdam Renaissance style to a design by Hendrick de Keyser, with a clock showing four faces and a carillon of bells. The name comes from the guard house beside it, which was used to mint coins in the 17th century. The building you see next to the tower today is a Neo-Renaissance replacement from 1885-1887. The carillon now has 38 bells, and it chimes every quarter of an hour. That makes the tower a nice subject for a short video as well as a still. The square is busy with trams, bikes and pedestrians, so expect people and traffic in your shots. Use them for a sense of place, or wait for a gap. Stand back far enough to fit the whole spire without tilting the phone too much, then move in for a second shot of the clock faces and spire detail. Check that the tower's vertical lines look straight against the gridlines before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: The Munttoren stands on Muntplein in central Amsterdam, where the Amstel river and the Singel canal meet. It is close to the flower market and the eastern end of the Kalverstraat shopping street.
text.directions_text: Trams are usually the easiest way in. The nearest stop is Keizersgracht (tram 17, tram 2, tram 24 and tram 4): the tower is to the north, about 4 minutes on foot. From Rembrandtplein tram stop (tram 14 and tram 4) the tower is to the west, about 4 minutes on foot. If you prefer the metro, go to Rokin (metro 52, plus tram 14 and tram 4): the tower is to the south, about 5 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower and the water or square around it. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spire, clock faces and brickwork. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a big sky and street scene, and keep the tower in the centre so its edges do not stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 45 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. From here the whole tower and its guard house should fit in an upright frame with the default lens (1x).
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and switch on the gridlines so the tower's sides run parallel to the vertical lines. Leave a little space above the spire. Include a tram, cyclist or bit of waterside in the foreground if you want a feeling of the busy square. For a close-up, zoom in on the open spire against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. If you are there when the bells chime, try a Live Photo or a short video to catch the sound and movement of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer, with fewer people and less traffic in the frame. At dusk, switch on night mode, hold the phone steady against a wall or railing, and the lit tower should stand out against the darker sky. On Saturdays between 2 and 3 pm there is a live carillon concert, which is good for video.

text.access_note: The tower stands on a busy public square, so you can photograph it from the street; check the official site before you go if you want to know about any other access.

text.description:
The Westerkerk is a big Protestant church on the western edge of the canal ring, just beside the Jordaan, between the Prinsengracht and the Keizersgracht. It was built between 1620 and 1631 to designs by Hendrick de Keyser and finished by his son Pieter. At about 58 metres long and 29 metres wide, it is still the largest church in the Netherlands built for Protestants. The real draw for a photo is the Westertoren, the tower, which at 87 metres is the tallest church tower in Amsterdam. It ends in a spire topped with the Imperial Crown of Austria of Maximilian I, a shape that is easy to recognise even in a small phone frame.

Because the tower is so tall, the main challenge is fitting it in without it looking squashed. Include a little of the street or canal edge in the foreground to give a sense of scale, and keep the phone upright and level so the walls do not lean inwards too much. Once you have the full view, switch to a zoom lens and take a tighter shot of the crown and upper tower. The brickwork and stone details look best in soft, even light. The church is still a working place of worship, so be considerate of anyone going in or out while you take your pictures.
text.geographic_location: The Westerkerk is in central Amsterdam, in the westernmost part of the Grachtengordel (canal ring) in the Centrum district. It sits between the Prinsengracht and the Keizersgracht, right next to the Jordaan. Its position on the map is the middle of the church's outline, which is about 76 m across.
text.directions_text: The easiest approach is by tram: from the Marnixplein tram stop (tram 13 or tram 5) the Westerkerk lies to the south-east, about 8 minutes on foot. From the Bloemgracht tram stop (also tram 13 or tram 5) it lies to the east, also about 8 minutes on foot. If you come by metro, Rokin (metro 52, tram 14 and tram 4) is the nearest station, with the church to the north-west, about 12 minutes on foot. Centraal Station (metro 51, metro 52, metro 53, metro 54, tram 2, tram 4, tram 14, tram 17, tram 24 and tram 26) is a longer walk, with the church to the west, about 20 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole church and tower into one frame from close range. Then use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the crown and upper tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Pick a spot with a clear, open view of the subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line. Keep the phone as upright as you can, because tilting it upwards makes the tower lean. Leave a little foreground at the bottom for scale, then take a second, tighter shot of the spire with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky stays blue and the brick keeps its detail. If you take a Live Photo, it can catch passing cyclists or boats.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the brick and stone, and tends to be calmer around the church.

text.access_note: The church is a working place of worship, so the interior and the tower may have visiting restrictions; check the official site before you go.
